label: First input is v/j/1; plus re-input of first token at first copy step in L=3 sequences
predicate: ((t == 0) & isin(in_tok, [tok("v"), tok("j"), tok("1")])) | ((L == 3) & (t == 4) & isin(in_tok, [tok("y"), tok("1"), tok("q"), tok("v"), tok("f"), tok("c"), tok("j")]))
explanation: Two related firing sites. (1) Step t=0 when the first original token is v, j or 1: about 8% of those steps are active, with no exceptions in precision, and this accounts for ~83% of activation mass. Magnitude depends on the token: 1 > v >> j (j steps carry about 0.02 of max, 1 carries most of the mass). (2) Length-3 sequences at t=4 (recall_idx 1), where the fed-back input is orig(0) and the output is orig(1). Here the rate depends on the token: y ~94%, 1 ~78%, q ~61%, v ~56%, f ~53%, c/j ~45%, and most other letters ~25% or lower. These are the strongest activations overall (y at L=3 t=4 is the max). It never fires at t=1..3, at the delimiter, or at copy steps other than t=4. It also never fires at t=4 for L>3. The two clauses share a theme: the unit responds to the first token of the sequence as an input when the hidden state is near-initial or short-context.  Leaving out the second clause gives precision 1.0 but mass recall of only 0.83.

dev_scores.predicate: ((t == 0) & isin(in_tok, [tok("v"), tok("j"), tok("1")])) | ((L == 3) & (t == 4) & isin(in_tok, [tok("y"), tok("1"), tok("q"), tok("v"), tok("f"), tok("c"), tok("j")]))

issues: The factual claims hold up on dev. Clause 1 has precision 1.0, recall 0.943 and mass recall 0.835. No activity at t=1..3, at the delimiter, or at copy steps other than t=4. Every t=4 activation is in an L=3 sequence (prev_tok=<DEL> accounts for all 600 of them). The per-token firing rates for clause 2 match the stated numbers (y 0.94, 1 0.78, q 0.61, v 0.56, f 0.53, c/j about 0.45), and the reported test scores reproduce (F1 0.979, mass recall 0.966).

Clause 2 is incomplete as described. At L=3, t=4, whether the unit fires also depends strongly on orig(1), which is the token being output, and on orig(2), not only on the input token. Precision drops to about 0.02-0.07 when orig(1) or orig(2) is one of h, i, j, m or v, and rises to 0.4-0.57 when either is one of f, s, t, r or g. So 'depends on which token is input' covers only part of it: this clause is a noisy conjunction of all three tokens.

The remaining errors (about 220 misses and 230 false positives on test, 3.4% of activation mass) all fall inside the L=3, t=4 region. They are small, and modelling them does not help much. Excluding output and orig(2) tokens with low firing rates and widening the input-token set only raises test F1 from 0.979 to 0.980-0.981.

The label does not overclaim relative to the predicate. The only weakness is that the 'first copy step in L=3' clause is approximate, and the description should say it also depends on orig(1) and orig(2).
